title: Chapter 24 — The Advocate
paragraphs: Since Queequeg and I are now properly launched in this business of whaling, and since whaling has somehow come to be seen by people on land as a rather unpoetic and disreputable trade, I am anxious to convince you landlubbers of the injustice done to us whale hunters.

First, it may seem unnecessary to establish the fact that, among the general public, whaling is not considered on the same level as the so-called liberal professions. If a stranger were introduced into any mixed gathering of city society, it would hardly raise the general opinion of his merits to present him as a harpooner. And if, in imitation of naval officers, he were to add the letters S.W.F. (Sperm Whale Fishery) after his name on his business card, that would be considered extremely presumptuous and ridiculous.

No doubt one main reason the world refuses to honor us whalemen is this: people think that our occupation amounts to a butchering sort of business, and that when we're actively at work, we're surrounded by filth and gore. Butchers we are — that's true. But butchers, too, and butchers of the bloodiest sort, have been all the military commanders whom the world loves to honor. And as for the alleged uncleanliness of our business, you'll soon learn certain facts generally unknown which will place the sperm whale ship among the cleanest operations on this tidy earth. But even granting the charge to be true — what messy, slippery decks of a whale ship can compare with the unspeakable carnage of those battlefields from which so many soldiers return to drink in the applause of ladies? And if the idea of danger so greatly enhances the popular admiration of the soldier's profession, let me assure you that many a veteran who has bravely marched toward a cannon battery would quickly turn and run at the sight of a sperm whale's vast tail churning the air above his head. For what are the dangers men can understand compared with the intertwined terrors and wonders of God!

But though the world looks down on us whale hunters, it unknowingly pays us the deepest tribute — indeed, an overwhelming devotion! For almost all the candles, lamps, and tapers that burn around the globe burn, like offerings before so many shrines, to our glory!
But look at this from other angles. Weigh it on every scale. See what we whalemen are and have been.

Why did the Dutch in De Witt's time have admirals of their whaling fleets? Why did Louis XVI of France personally fund whaling ships from Dunkirk, and politely invite a couple dozen families from our own island of Nantucket to that town? Why did Britain, between 1750 and 1788, pay its whalemen over one million pounds in bounties? And finally, how is it that American whalemen now outnumber all the other whalemen in the world combined, sailing a fleet of over seven hundred vessels, manned by eighteen thousand men, spending four million dollars a year, with ships worth twenty million dollars at the time of sailing, and importing a well-harvested seven million dollars into our harbors annually? How do you explain all this, if there isn't something mighty in whaling?
But that's only half of it. Look again.

I assert freely that the most worldly philosopher cannot, for the life of him, point to one single peaceful influence that, within the last sixty years, has had more powerful impact on the entire world, taken as a whole, than the grand business of whaling. One way and another, it has produced events so remarkable in themselves, and so endlessly significant in their consequences, that whaling may well be compared to that mythical Egyptian mother who bore children already pregnant in the womb. It would be a hopeless, endless task to list them all. A handful will do. For many years the whale ship has been the pioneer in discovering the most remote and least known parts of the earth. She has explored seas and island chains that had no chart, where no Cook or Vancouver had ever sailed. If American and European warships now ride peacefully in once-savage harbors, let them fire salutes to the honor of the whale ship, which showed them the way and first served as interpreter with the natives. They may celebrate the heroes of exploring expeditions — your Cooks, your Krusensterns — but I say that scores of unnamed captains have sailed out of Nantucket who were as great, and greater, than Cook and Krusenstern. In their helpless, empty-handed state, in shark-infested waters and on the beaches of uncharted islands, they battled with unknown dangers and wonders that Cook, with all his marines and muskets, would not have willingly faced. All the feats that fill three chapters in the old South Sea voyage accounts were just everyday life for our heroic Nantucketers. Adventures that Vancouver devoted whole chapters to, these men didn't consider worth noting in the ship's log. Ah, the world! Oh, the world!

Until the whale fishery rounded Cape Horn, no trade but colonial, and hardly any contact but colonial, existed between Europe and the long line of wealthy Spanish provinces on the Pacific coast. It was the whaleman who first broke through the jealous trade policies of the Spanish crown regarding those colonies. And if space allowed, it could be clearly shown how the efforts of those whalemen eventually led to the liberation of Peru, Chile, and Bolivia from the yoke of Spain, and the establishment of democracy in those lands.

That great America on the other side of the globe, Australia, was opened to the civilized world by the whaleman. After its first accidental discovery by a Dutchman, all other ships long avoided those shores as dangerously savage. But the whale ship went there. The whale ship is the true mother of that now mighty nation. In the early days of the first Australian settlement, the colonists were several times saved from starvation by the generous provisions of whale ships that happened to anchor in their waters. The countless islands of Polynesia tell the same story, owing a commercial debt to the whale ship that cleared the way for missionaries and merchants, and in many cases actually carried the first missionaries to their destinations. If that sealed-off nation, Japan, is ever to become welcoming, it is the whale ship alone that will deserve the credit — for she is already at the doorstep.
But if, despite all this, you still insist that whaling has no noble or artistic associations, then I am ready to break fifty lances with you right here, and knock you off your horse every time.
The whale has no famous author, and whaling no famous chronicler, you say.

The whale no famous author, and whaling no famous chronicler? Who wrote the first account of our great Leviathan? None other than mighty Job! And who composed the first whaling narrative? No less a prince than Alfred the Great, who with his own royal pen took down the words of Ohthere, the Norwegian whale hunter of those times! And who delivered our glowing praise in Parliament? Edmund Burke!
True enough, you say, but whalemen themselves are lowly types with no noble blood.

No noble blood? They have something better than royal blood. The grandmother of Benjamin Franklin was Mary Morrel, later Mary Folger by marriage, one of the original settlers of Nantucket and ancestor to a long line of Folgers and harpooners — all kin to noble Benjamin — to this day hurling the barbed iron from one side of the world to the other.
Fine, you say, but everyone agrees that whaling somehow just isn't respectable.
Whaling not respectable? Whaling is imperial! By old English law, the whale is officially declared "a royal fish."
Oh, that's only a technicality! The whale itself has never figured in anything grand or imposing.

The whale never figured in anything grand or imposing? In one of the mighty triumphs staged for a Roman general upon his entry into the world's capital, the bones of a whale, brought all the way from the Syrian coast, were the most prominent objects in the cymbal-clashing procession.
See later chapters for more on this subject.
All right, since you bring it up. But say what you will, there's no real dignity in whaling.

No dignity in whaling? The very heavens proclaim the dignity of our calling. Cetus is a constellation in the southern sky! Enough said! Bow your head before the Czar, but take off your hat to Queequeg! Enough! I know a man who has taken three hundred and fifty whales in his lifetime. I consider that man more honorable than the great ancient general who boasted of capturing as many walled cities.

And as for me, if there's any undiscovered quality worth noting in me, if I ever deserve any real reputation in that small but lofty world I might reasonably aspire to, if I ever accomplish anything that a man might rather have done than left undone, if when I die my executors — or more accurately, my creditors — find any valuable manuscripts in my desk, then I give all the honor and glory to whaling. For a whale ship was my Yale College and my Harvard.
